newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Foreign buyers seen for Thai finance firms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Foreign buyers seen for Thai finance firms.

text.p: Thailand's troubled but cheap finance sector is likely to attract bargain-hunters now that the government has eased constraints on foreign equity participation, analysts said on Thursday.

But investors are unlikely to jump into actual deals until a clearer picture emerges of the firms' asset quality and details of measures announced on Wednesday to save the crisis-hit finance sector, they said.

"The measures are heading in the right direction. Thailand needs such inflows to avert financial meltdown. But there are some details that the authorities need to spell out," said Arporn Chewakrengkai of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"What the government announced on Wednesday was quite broad. Investors are not likely to do anything unless they see strong incentive," she added.

In urgent decrees announced on Tuesday aimed at stabilising the beleaguered finance sector, the government said it would allow foreign investors to hold more than 25 percent in finance firms and banks that emerged from finance firm mergers.
Thailand had previously capped foreign ownership in banks and finance firms at 25 percent.
A new ceiling was not set and will be decided at the central bank's discretion based on shareholder structure.

The authorities also issued decrees to smooth out the process of merging finance companies to transfer doubtful loan accounts, waive taxes and transaction fees arising from mergers and authorise companies to hold extra shareholders meetings to approve corporate alliances.
They also barred creditors of merging finance firms from seeking court orders to stop proposed corporate alliances among these firms.
Industry sources said despite problems plaguing the finance sector, investors from Asia, Europe and the United States had already expressed interest in buying Thai companies.
GE Capital Corp of the United States, for example, was said to be set to buy into a medium-sized Thai finance firm. Malaysian firms have also been making inquiries, the sources said.

"Many foreign investors who are interested in investing here require a controlling stake. That's why they are reluctant to invest in the sector in the past...besides it is cheap to enter the market here," said a senior investment banker at Dhana Siam Finance and Securities.
The Thai stock index has plunged more than 60 percent over the past year with banks and finance firms hardest hit.

"The short-term outlook for the finance sector might look bleak, but measures prescribed to them such as provisions on non-performing loans and incentives to merge will make the sector stronger in the future," the investment banker said.
However, other analysts said that although the measures were good, their effect on the cash-strapped sector would be limited.

"With the non-performing loans problem escalating, investors can never be sure about the asset quality of the finance sector. Of course, they can do a due diligence but there are always accounting methods to mask the real situation," said an analyst at a major US investment bank.
Private sector estimates put the extent of finance company non-performing loans now at 31.5 percent of all outstanding loans.
"There are 91 finance firms in the sector, about a third in deep trouble. Investors are likely to be very selective and limit investment to a few with good prospects," the analyst said.
